title: Heaven's net
hook: heaven's net is wide and loose, yet nothing slips through (Tao Te Ching 73)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the week with don't crowd them. Your line was give room. Did someone come to you in their own time? A new week starts now. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

A fishing net hangs drying on a fence. The holes are big enough to put a fist through. It looks like it couldn't hold anything. Water runs straight through it. And yet, cast the right way, at the right depth, it comes back full. Chapter seventy-three of the Tao Te Ching hangs a net like that over the whole world. Before it gets there, it talks about two kinds of courage.
screen: `A NET WITH WIDE HOLES.` → `IT STILL COMES BACK FULL.` → `TWO KINDS OF COURAGE.`

segments.voice: First, the two kinds of courage. The chapter says: bold in daring, and you're killed. Bold in not daring, and you live. One brings benefit, one brings harm. And then it shrugs: what heaven dislikes, who knows the reason? Even the sage finds this hard. That honesty matters. The chapter doesn't pretend the world's workings are easy to read. Second, how heaven's way works. It doesn't fight, yet it's good at winning. It doesn't speak, yet it's good at answering. It isn't summoned, yet it comes on its own. It seems slack, unhurried, yet it plans well. Every line pairs an absence with a result. Third, the net. Heaven's net is vast, its mesh is wide, and yet nothing is lost. That's the picture to keep. The net isn't tight. It doesn't grab or chase. And still nothing falls out of it. Readers have taken this a few ways: as a promise that things come back around, as a reassurance that the world holds together without our clutching, or as a warning that nothing done is really hidden. The chapter doesn't pick for us. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. A lot of worry is an attempt to tighten the mesh. To check every thread, control every outcome, close every gap ourselves. Heaven's net is a different picture: loose, patient, and holding. Not every result will be the one we want. But the clutching isn't what holds it.
screen: `DARING, OR NOT DARING.` · `NO FIGHT, YET IT WINS.` · `WIDE MESH, NOTHING LOST.` · `LOOSEN THE GRIP.` · then, large: `HEAVEN'S NET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust one thing to work out. Sit, and let the breath come and go without managing it. Bring to mind one thing you've been gripping: a result you're waiting on, a situation you keep checking. Picture it resting in a wide net, holes and all. You've done your part. Now, for these two minutes, let the net hold it. When the urge to check or fix comes back, notice it, and let the mesh stay loose. The bell holds the time.
Heaven's net. Chapter seventy-three: vast, wide-meshed, and yet nothing slips through. Today's word.
Your line: heaven's net. Today, when you reach to check something again, let it rest one more hour in the net. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-three's wide-meshed net as a picture of a world that holds together without force, and some read it as a reminder that nothing done stays hidden.

myth: chapter seventy-three says heaven's net is fine and tight
it says the net is vast and wide-meshed, and yet nothing is lost.
the chapter admits even the sage finds heaven's reasons hard
what heaven dislikes, it asks, who knows why? even the sage finds it hard.
the chapter says heaven's way comes without being summoned
it isn't called, yet it comes on its own.

fork.setup: you're facing a risk. chapter seventy-three names two kinds of courage. which one does it say leads to life?
fork.reveal: bold in daring, and you're killed; bold in not daring, and you live. then the chapter admits nobody fully knows heaven's reasons.

original.note: Chinese: heaven's net is vast, from chapter seventy-three.

trapdoor: what you thought: heaven's net is about getting caught.
what it means: the world holds things together loosely, without force, and nothing truly falls out.
what a scholar hears: the next words are 疏而不失, wide-meshed yet losing nothing; readers take it as reassurance, warning, or both.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 73 (courage in daring and in not daring; who knows what heaven dislikes; heaven's way does not contend yet wins; heaven's net is vast and wide-meshed yet loses nothing)

notes: Chapter 73 is paraphrased; the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording.
The three ways readers take the net (things come back around, reassurance, warning that nothing is hidden) are the writer's summary of common readings; confirm they are fair.
Original 天網恢恢 (tiān wǎng huī huī) rendered 'TYEN wahng HWAY hway'; trapdoor cites 疏而不失 (Wang Bi text). Confirm.
Editor: replaced the stock line 'a whole worldview folded into that net' and the 'starts, though, somewhere sharper' turn, which echoed day 1132's hook structure.
